title: The Second World War

cards.h: The deadliest war in history, in five dates
cards.b:
On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Britain and France declared war two days later. Over six years, the war killed an estimated 70-85 million people, most of them civilians.

Here is the story in the fewest possible steps.
Germany's fast attack, Blitzkrieg, conquered Poland and then France in six weeks (1940). Britain held out in the Battle of Britain, with Churchill's leadership.

In June 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union. On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and the US entered the war. The Soviets beat Germany at Stalingrad (1942-43). The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people.

In June 1944 Allied forces landed in Normandy (D-Day, 6 June). Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945.

The US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August). Japan announced surrender on 15 August; the formal signing was on 2 September. Historians still argue about whether the bombs were needed, or whether the Soviet entry into the war was decisive.

Cities lay in ruins, and tens of millions were displaced. The war gave birth to the United Nations (1945), the Nuremberg trials, and a world with two superpowers, the US and USSR. It also made colonial empires harder to hold.

cards.h: Did the war start only in Europe in 1939?
cards.b: Myth: WWII started with Poland.Fact: in Asia, Japan invaded China in 1937 (or Manchuria in 1931), so for China the war began earlier. Also, Allied victory was not only the work of the US and Britain: the Soviet Union and China bore enormous losses.
An army, a famine and a movement

Five things to remember

  1. WWII began in 1939 (earlier in Asia).
  2. Germany attacked the USSR in 1941; Pearl Harbor drew in the US.
  3. D-Day 1944; Germany surrendered May 1945.
  4. Atomic bombs preceded Japan's surrender in August 1945.
  5. India contributed troops and suffered a famine.

Think about it

  • Was the bombing of cities justified?
  • How did the war speed up decolonisation?
